title: What is conditional aggregation, and how do you use `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` (or MySQL's `SUM(bool_expr)`) to answer "find customers who have BOTH a completed AND a cancelled order" or to pivot rows into columns — in a single grouped pass instead of multiple self-joins?
topicTitle: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM

s1_definition.profdef: Conditional aggregation applies an aggregate function over a `CASE` expression so that only rows meeting a condition contribute. `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts matching rows per group, and comparing several such expressions in a `HAVING` lets you test combined conditions like "has both a completed and a cancelled order" in one grouped pass, avoiding multiple self-joins or repeated subqueries.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at National Bank of India going through each customer's order pile exactly once. For every order, the clerk makes a tick in a "completed" column if it is completed, and a tick in a "cancelled" column if it is cancelled. At the end, a customer who has at least one tick in both columns is the one who has both a completed and a cancelled order. One pass through the pile answers a question that would otherwise need joining the pile to itself.
s1_definition.oneliner: Conditional aggregation uses `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` to count or pivot per group in a single pass, replacing self-joins and multiple subqueries.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Conditional aggregation applies an aggregate function over a `CASE` expression so that only rows meeting a condition contribute. `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts matching rows per group, and comparing several such expressions in a `HAVING` lets you test combined conditions like "has both a completed and a cancelled order" in one grouped pass, avoiding multiple self-joins or repeated subqueries.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at National Bank of India going through each customer's order pile exactly once. For every order, the clerk makes a tick in a "completed" column if it is completed, and a tick in a "cancelled" column if it is cancelled. At the end, a customer who has at least one tick in both columns is the one who has both a completed and a cancelled order. One pass through the pile answers a question that would otherwise need joining the pile to itself.

**One line to remember:** Conditional aggregation uses `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` to count or pivot per group in a single pass, replacing self-joins and multiple subqueries.

sections.s2_technical:
The idea is to push a condition inside the aggregate. `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` produces, per group, the count of rows where the status is completed, because each matching row contributes 1 and each non-matching row contributes 0. You can equally use `COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN 1 END)` since the `CASE` yields NULL for non-matching rows and `COUNT` ignores NULLs. In MySQL a boolean expression is treated as 1 or 0, so `SUM(status = 'COMPLETED')` works as a shorthand.

To answer "customers who have both a completed and a cancelled order," you group by customer and count each status conditionally, then filter in `HAVING`: `HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status='COMPLETED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0 AND SUM(CASE WHEN status='CANCELLED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0`. Each customer's orders are scanned once, both counters are built in the same pass, and the `HAVING` keeps only customers with at least one of each. The alternative without conditional aggregation is to join the orders table to itself — one copy filtered to completed, another to cancelled — or to run two `EXISTS` subqueries, both of which do more work.

Conditional aggregation also implements pivots, as covered earlier: `SUM(CASE WHEN channel='ATM' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)` becomes an ATM column. The technique generalizes to any per-group question that mixes conditions: "how many high-value versus low-value transactions per account," "revenue from each product line per region," "count of each order status per customer." The big advantages are a single table scan instead of multiple, readable standard SQL that runs on every engine, and the ability to compute many conditional measures side by side. A senior nuance is that you should prefer `SUM(CASE ...)` returning explicit 1/0 over clever tricks so the intent is obvious, and that for existence-only tests (does at least one exist) a `MAX(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` can be marginally cheaper than a full `SUM`.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's compliance team wants customers who have both a COMPLETED and a CANCELLED order, because that pattern can indicate payment manipulation. A junior wrote a self-join of orders to orders, which was slow and produced duplicate rows needing a DISTINCT. Conditional aggregation answers it in one grouped pass.

Problem 2 — The same team wants, per customer, a breakdown of how many orders are completed, cancelled, and pending, side by side. That is a conditional-aggregation pivot in a single query.

Our mini-project builds an `OrderPatternService` that computes per-customer status counts with conditional aggregation and filters for the both-completed-and-cancelled pattern, all in one pass. It includes a `Order` model, a repository, the service, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: six orders — C1 has COMPLETED, CANCELLED, PENDING; C2 has two COMPLETED; C3 has one CANCELLED.

Step 1 — The service makes one pass over all six orders. For each order it finds or creates the customer's counter bundle and increments the matching status counter, which is exactly the `SUM(CASE WHEN status = ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` behaviour expressed procedurally. Non-matching statuses contribute nothing, like the `ELSE 0`.

Step 2 — After the single pass, C1's counters are completed 1, cancelled 1, pending 1. C2's are completed 2, cancelled 0, pending 0. C3's are completed 0, cancelled 1, pending 0. All computed in one scan, no self-join.

Step 3 — The both-completed-and-cancelled filter applies the `HAVING` logic: keep a customer only if their completed count exceeds zero and their cancelled count exceeds zero. C1 has one of each, so C1 matches. C2 has completed but no cancelled, so it fails. C3 has cancelled but no completed, so it fails. Only C1 qualifies.

Step 4 — The result is C1, the single customer exhibiting the both-statuses pattern, found without any self-join or repeated subquery.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Conditional aggregation means applying an aggregate function over a `CASE` expression so that only the rows meeting a condition contribute to the result. The canonical form is `SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which produces, per group, the count of rows that satisfy the condition, because every matching row contributes one and every non-matching row contributes zero. You can equivalently write `COUNT(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 END)` since the `CASE` yields NULL for non-matching rows and `COUNT` skips NULLs, and in MySQL a boolean expression counts as one or zero so `SUM(status = 'COMPLETED')` is a shorthand.

The power of the technique is answering combined-condition questions in a single grouped pass. To find customers who have both a completed and a cancelled order, at the National Bank of India we group orders by customer, build a completed counter and a cancelled counter in the same scan, and then filter in `HAVING` for both counters being greater than zero. Each customer's orders are read once, both conditional counts are accumulated together, and the `HAVING` keeps only those with at least one of each status. The alternative without conditional aggregation is to join the orders table to itself, one copy filtered to completed and another to cancelled, or to run two separate `EXISTS` subqueries, both of which scan more and the self-join even produces duplicate rows needing a `DISTINCT`.

The same technique implements pivots, turning row values into columns, and it generalizes to any per-group question that mixes conditions, such as counting high-value versus low-value transactions per account or breaking down each order status side by side. Its advantages are a single table scan instead of several, plain standard SQL that runs on every engine, and the ability to compute many conditional measures together in one query. A couple of senior points I always add are that I prefer the explicit `SUM(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` form so the intent is unmistakable, and that for a pure existence test a `MAX(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` can be marginally cheaper. The line I always state is that conditional aggregation uses `SUM(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` to count or pivot per group in a single pass, replacing self-joins and multiple subqueries.

keyPoints: GROUP BY: group rows by column values
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
HAVING: filter groups (vs WHERE which filters rows)
GROUP BY + HAVING vs WHERE: WHERE runs first, HAVING runs after grouping
